resources.string: What is the MT_SW Planner

The MT_SW Planner helps you judge whether two points (A and B) can “hear” each other over LoRa radio, and how far a single station reaches. It calculates three things: the path loss (how much power the signal loses on the way), the power arriving at the receiver, and the margin against the receiver sensitivity, i.e. how many decibels (dB) remain above the minimum needed for reception.

How it works: the app fetches the terrain profile between A and B from the Mapterhorn elevation model, takes Earth curvature into account (k-factor, 4/3 by default), the antenna heights and the frequency, and then the Longley-Rice model (ITM) predicts the path loss. Starting from the transmit power the planner adds the antenna gains, subtracts cable and connector losses, adds an optional allowance for forest or buildings, and compares the result with the sensitivity computed from bandwidth, spreading factor and receiver noise figure.

Example: two nodes 10 km apart with a clear line of sight, 868 MHz, 20 dBm, 2.15 dBi antennas, Narrow Fast preset (sensitivity about −127.5 dBm). Free-space loss is about 111 dB, received power about −87 dBm, margin about 40 dB. The same setup behind a hill or in dense forest can end up with a margin close to zero.

Getting started: 1) pick points A and B (a node, the map, typed coordinates or your own station), 2) set antenna heights, power, gains and cables, 3) choose the band and the modem preset your radios really use (in the MT_SW network of the Świętokrzyskie region: 868 MHz and Narrow presets), 4) read the verdict, the profile chart and the margin, 5) improve the cheapest things first: antenna height, then cable and antenna, power last. Every parameter has its own info card.

Honesty of the result: this is a statistical prediction, not a measurement. ITM returns a median value; the real signal at a given moment typically differs from it by ±6–10 dB, and more in difficult terrain. Forest and buildings are only represented by a fixed extra attenuation, and the terrain model does not see individual trees, houses and poles. Treat the result as a starting point: plan for a margin of at least 10 dB and test important links in the field. If you have a measured SNR and RSSI, compare it with the prediction (the “Comparison with measurement” card).
Points A and B

Point A and point B are the two ends of the link. You can set the coordinates in four ways: by choosing a mesh node with a known position, by tapping the map, by typing latitude and longitude (decimal degrees, WGS-84, latitude first), or by using your own station, i.e. the connected radio.

The accuracy of a point carries over into the result. A node position from the mesh may be rounded (position precision set on the channel), and GPS inside a building can be off by tens of metres. On a 10 km path such an error does not change the free-space loss, but near a hilltop or an embankment it changes the terrain height by several to a dozen metres, and that already affects diffraction. For a mast on a summit, mark the point precisely on the map, not “roughly”.

The position of your own station may be unavailable: the radio has no GPS fix yet or is not connected. The planner then shows a hint and you have to set the point by hand. If a node's position is deliberately blurred, treat the result as indicative.

Common mistakes: swapped latitude and longitude (for the Świętokrzyskie region latitude is about 50.5–51.3 and longitude about 19.7–21.8), a comma instead of a decimal point, and point B at the same place as A. When the points are closer than 10 m the planner reports a “points too close” error.

Limit: the planner calculates a two-point link along a straight line on a sphere. Obstacles that are not in the terrain model are not taken into account.
Ground elevation (ASL)

Ground elevation is the height of the ground at the point above sea level. The planner fetches it automatically from the Mapterhorn terrain model and uses it to build the whole profile between A and B. Set it by hand only when you know better than the model.

Effect on the result: what matters is not the absolute value but the difference against the terrain along the path. The model grid has a resolution of some tens of metres, so it smooths summits and fills narrow valleys. If the model underestimates the summit where your mast stands, the prediction will be too pessimistic; if it overestimates, too optimistic. A manual value replaces the terrain sample at that one point only; the rest of the profile stays from the model.

How to set it in practice: leave it on automatic unless the difference is obvious. Enter a manual value when you know the elevation from a topographic map, a survey or Geoportal (NMT). The altitude from a phone GPS can be wrong by 10–30 m, so without verification it is no better than the model.

Common mistakes: entering the antenna altitude ASL (e.g. 280 m) instead of the height above ground, or adding the mast height twice. Ground elevation is the ground, not the roof: enter a building or mast height in the antenna height field.

Limit: the terrain model usually does not contain trees and buildings. In some regions the source data may however describe the surface rather than the bare ground, so if it disagrees with a map, verify the elevation manually.
Antenna height

Antenna height is the height of its centre above the ground at that point, not ASL and not relative to a roof (unless the roof is your ground, in which case add the building height). The default is 2 m, i.e. a radio held in the hand or on a low tripod.

Effect on the result: height decides whether the path has line of sight and how far the radio horizon reaches. For k = 4/3 the horizon is roughly 4.12·(√h1 + √h2) km with heights in metres. For 2 m and 2 m that is about 12 km, for 10 m and 2 m about 19 km, for 30 m and 2 m about 28 km. Beyond the horizon the loss rises fast because diffraction starts to dominate.

In the Świętokrzyskie region, where paths cross hills and forests, the biggest gain usually comes from raising the antenna above the treetops and out of the shadow of a ridge. Going from 2 m to 10 m often gains several to a dozen dB, from 10 m to 20 m less. Raise the antenna on the side where the obstacle is closer: there each metre gives the most clearance.

Note: on a path with a clear line of sight the free-space loss does not depend on height; height only improves the Fresnel clearance.

Common mistakes: height measured from the wrong level (e.g. from a roof when the surrounding ground is lower), and an antenna on a building wall entered as 2 m even though the direction behind the building is shielded. An accuracy of ±1 m is usually enough. When heights fall outside the range the model considers sensible, ITM raises warnings and the result is less reliable.
Transmit power

You enter the transmit power in dBm, a logarithmic scale: 20 dBm is 100 mW, 22 dBm is about 158 mW, 27 dBm is 500 mW and 30 dBm is 1 W. The planner also shows the conversion to watts. Every +3 dB is twice the power, +10 dB is ten times.

Effect on the result is direct: power adds to the budget dB for dB (received power = power + antenna gains − cable losses − path loss). Raising 20 dBm to 27 dBm gives +7 dB of margin, which in free space means about 2.2 times the range, but in forest or behind a hill much less, because diffraction loss grows faster.

How to set it: enter the power the radio is actually configured to in its LoRa settings, not the catalogue maximum. The power at the antenna connector depends on the radio chip and the supply; the nominal value can differ from the real one.

Common mistake: high power on one side only. A mesh link works in both directions (acknowledgements, routing), so the weaker direction decides everything. The planner calculates A→B and B→A separately; look at the worse one. High power does not improve your own receiver's sensitivity and it increases interference for others.

Regulations: the permitted power in the 868 MHz band depends on the sub-band and is sometimes specified as ERP or EIRP, so antenna gain counts too. Check the current rules and the region setting in the device. This is not legal advice.
Antenna gain (dBi)

Antenna gain in dBi tells how much the antenna concentrates energy compared with an ideal omnidirectional antenna. A dipole has 2.15 dBi (the default value), and dBd = dBi − 2.15. Gain does not create power, it redirects it: a higher-gain omni antenna squeezes the beam in the vertical plane, while a Yagi or panel also squeezes it horizontally.

Effect on the result: the gains of the transmitting and receiving antennas add to the budget dB for dB. An extra 3 dBi equals doubling the power.

Typical values at 868 MHz: a short rubber duck or pigtail antenna realistically −2 to +2 dBi (manufacturers often overstate); a collinear omni 3–6 dBi; a Yagi 8–12 dBi; a panel 9–14 dBi. It is safest to enter a value 2–3 dB below the catalogue figure, or one based on measurement.

Pitfalls: a high-gain omni antenna has a narrow vertical beam (some ten degrees), so on a hilltop it may overshoot the valleys below. In hills higher gain does not always win. The planner does not model the radiation pattern: it assumes a directional antenna is aimed at the other end and that both antennas are vertically polarised. An antenna turned to horizontal polarisation against the other one adds a loss of even 15–20 dB that you will not see in the result.

Enter gain without cable loss. Cable and connectors are set separately, in the cable loss card.
Cable and connector loss

The feeder is everything between the radio and the antenna: cable, adapters and connectors. Each element absorbs part of the power both when transmitting and when receiving. In simple mode you enter the total loss in dB; the default is 0 dB, i.e. the antenna sits directly on the radio.

Effect on the result: the feeder loss at one end lowers the margin by that many dB in both directions (it weakens the power sent from that end and the power received at that end). Losses at both ends add up. 3 dB is half the power.

Typical values at 868 MHz (approximate): a 20 cm U.FL-to-SMA pigtail of thin RG316 cable with its connectors about 0.3 dB; 1 m of RG316 about 0.8 dB; 10 m of LMR-400 about 1.3 dB (about 0.13 dB/m); 20 m of LMR-400 about 2.6 dB plus connectors. Thin RG174 or RG58 over a few metres is already 3–5 dB.

Most common mistake: forgetting the pigtail and adapters (0.1–0.5 dB each) and a thin cable stub right at the radio. If you know the parts, use precise mode, because it accounts for lengths and frequency.

Limits: the planner does not model antenna mismatch (VSWR), ageing or moisture in the cable. The real loss of an old, wet cable is higher than the catalogue figure.
Cable and connector calculator

Precise mode builds the feeder from blocks: you choose the number of connectors (up to 8), and between them cable sections with a length. There are ready-made sets: direct, U.FL-to-SMA pigtail, pigtail with 10 m of LMR-400, pigtail with 20 m of LMR-400, Ecoflex 10 on a roof (15 m) and Heliax LDF4-50A on a mast (40 m). You can also choose a custom cable and enter its attenuation in dB/m.

The planner sums the connector losses (typical values for a mated pair, frequency dependent) and the cable losses, i.e. attenuation in dB/m at your frequency times length. The attenuation comes from the manufacturers' data sheets and is interpolated between the measured points. The result is itemised line by line, so you can see which element dominates.

How to set it: trace the path from the radio to the antenna, e.g. radio, U.FL pigtail, SMA connector, cable, N connector, antenna. Add every section with its real length. At 868 MHz this is typically tenths of a dB per connector and from a few tenths to over 1 dB per metre of thin cable.

The “approximate” label appears when the cable or connector data is second-hand, rounded, sparse or does not reach your frequency. For U.FL, MHF4, MMCX, UHF connectors and adapters the values are typical, not guaranteed.

Common mistakes: choosing the wrong cable type (thin RG58 instead of LMR-400 or RG213), a forgotten adapter and a length entered by eye. Limits: no model of mismatch, ageing and moisture.
Frequency and band

The operating frequency affects the free-space loss (it grows by 6 dB when the frequency doubles), the size of the Fresnel zone (it shrinks with the square root of frequency) and the behaviour of vegetation and terrain (a higher frequency means more attenuation by leaves and weaker diffraction). The planner knows the 169, 433 (ISM), 470, 868 (EU), 915, 923 and 2400 MHz bands and a free mode of 20–20000 MHz, the range in which ITM is valid.

For the MT_SW network (Świętokrzyskie region, 868 MHz) choose the 868 band. The default frequency is 869.44165 MHz. If your radio uses a different slot, enter its frequency. The difference within 863–870 MHz is fractions of a dB and usually does not matter, but it is better to have the real value.

Example: the same 10 km path has a free-space loss of about 105 dB at 433 MHz, about 111 dB at 868 MHz and about 120 dB at 2.4 GHz. That is why 868 MHz is a good compromise between range and antenna size.

Common mistakes: entering the frequency in other units (the field expects MHz), and assuming the planner checks regulations: the permitted power and duty cycle depend on the sub-band and are not verified here.

Note: above 1 GHz the planner additionally adds atmospheric gas and rain attenuation. At 868 MHz it is negligible and is not calculated.
Modem preset (BW and SF)

A modem preset is a set of LoRa parameters. The planner takes two numbers from it for the budget: the bandwidth (BW) and the spreading factor (SF). They determine the receiver sensitivity and the noise level (see the “Receiver sensitivity” card). Choose the same preset your radios actually use on this path; both ends must use the same one.

The most common presets and their sensitivity at a 6 dB noise figure: Narrow Fast 62.5 kHz, SF7, about −127.5 dBm; Narrow Slow 62.5 kHz, SF8, about −130.0 dBm; Lite Fast 125 kHz, SF9, about −129.5 dBm; Lite Slow 125 kHz, SF10, about −132.0 dBm; Long Fast 250 kHz, SF11, about −131.5 dBm; Tiny Fast and Tiny Slow (15.625 kHz, SF7 and SF8) about −133.6 and −136.1 dBm.

Practical conclusion: every SF step up improves sensitivity by 2.5 dB at the cost of longer airtime, and a narrower bandwidth means less noise and interference. The difference between Narrow Fast and Narrow Slow is 2.5 dB, i.e. about 1.3 times the free-space range.

You can also override BW and SF by hand; the preset is then no longer selected. The coding rate (CR) does not affect the planner result.

Common mistake: checking a link on a long-range preset when the network runs a Narrow preset. The result is then too optimistic by about 4 dB.
Receiver sensitivity

Sensitivity is the weakest signal the receiver can still decode. The planner computes it from: sensitivity (dBm) = −174 + 10·log10(BW in Hz) + NF + SNR limit for the SF. The terms: −174 dBm/Hz is thermal noise, 10·log10(BW) scales it by the bandwidth, NF is the receiver noise figure (6 dB by default), and the SNR limit is the lowest signal-to-noise ratio at which that SF still works. According to the Semtech data sheets it is: SF5 −2.5, SF6 −5, SF7 −7.5, SF8 −10, SF9 −12.5, SF10 −15, SF11 −17.5, SF12 −20 dB.

Example: Narrow Fast (62.5 kHz, SF7): 10·log10(62500) = 48.0, so −174 + 48.0 + 6 − 7.5 = −127.5 dBm. The noise level without the SNR term is −120 dBm. LoRa can receive a signal below the noise level, which is exactly why the SNR limit is negative.

Effect on the result: sensitivity is the threshold against which the margin is computed, so 3 dB better sensitivity is the same as 3 dB more power.

How to set NF: 6 dB is a reasonable value for typical SX126x chips (the field accepts 0–30 dB). A module with a good LNA and filter may reach 4–5 dB, a cheap module or a noisy environment more.

Honesty: in a city and with interference (switching power supplies, other transmitters in the ISM band) the real noise level is higher than thermal, even by 10–20 dB, and the effective sensitivity is worse. The value shown is the theoretical sensitivity from data sheets, so keep a margin and compare with a measurement.
K-factor and Earth curvature

Radio waves bend slightly downwards in the atmosphere, so the Earth “appears” less curved than it really is. This is described by the k-factor (effective Earth radius = k times 6371 km). The standard value is 4/3, about 1.33, and the planner uses it by default.

Effect on the result: k changes the Earth bulge on the profile chart, the Fresnel clearance and the elevation angles. The bulge at mid-path is d²/(8·k·R). On a 30 km path it is about 13 m for k = 4/3, about 18 m for k = 1 and about 26 m for k = 2/3. On paths up to 10 km the difference is about half a metre, practically irrelevant. The ITM loss itself depends on the surface refractivity N0 (301 N-units by default), not directly on k.

How it is set in practice: without weather the planner uses k = 4/3 and N0 = 301. With weather enabled it derives k and N0 from the forecast refractivity gradient (see the “Weather and refraction” card). The values are limited to sensible ranges (k from 0.5 to 20, N0 from 250 to 400).

Common mistake: assuming the atmosphere is always standard. With k below 4/3 (sub-refraction) the radio horizon shortens, with k above 4/3 (super-refraction) it lengthens.

Honesty: k changes over the day and the year, and a single number does not describe thin inversion layers, which can extend range by tens or hundreds of kilometres.
Weather and refraction

The weather option fetches current conditions at the middle of the path from the internet (Open-Meteo): temperature, humidity and pressure at the surface, precipitation, and temperature, humidity and height at the 925, 850 and 700 hPa levels. From this the planner computes the radio refractivity N (per ITU-R P.453) and its vertical gradient between the ground and the level nearest to 1 km above it. From that it derives the k-factor, the refractivity N0 for ITM (range 250–400, default 301) and a ducting assessment.

Ducting assessment: a gradient above −79 N/km is normal (the standard atmosphere is −39.2 N/km); from −157 to −79 N/km is elevated refraction (super-refraction, slightly longer range); below −157 N/km is a possible tropospheric duct.

The effect at 868 MHz is usually small: N0 changes the ITM loss by fractions of a dB up to a few dB, and gas and rain attenuation is only calculated above 1 GHz. The option mainly serves to judge whether today's conditions differ from normal.

Honesty: the 925, 850 and 700 hPa levels are thick layers (roughly 0.7, 1.5 and 3 km ASL), so thin inversions near the ground, typical in valleys at night and under high pressure, are invisible. The forecast describes one point and one moment. It is an indicative measure, not a ducting model, and it does not predict over-the-horizon ranges.

Tropospheric propagation data from other sites cannot be embedded in the app. For your own orientation you may look at the independent page https://www.dxinfocentre.com/tropo_eur.html (tropo forecasts for Europe), for personal use. The app does not use its data and is not affiliated with it.

Without internet the planner falls back to k = 4/3 and N0 = 301. Weather data: Open-Meteo.com (CC BY 4.0).
Forest and buildings (extra attenuation)

The ITM model knows the shape of the terrain, but not forests or buildings. That is why the planner has an extra attenuation field (in dB) that is added to the path loss. Presets: none 0 dB, open terrain 0 dB, light forest 3 dB, dense forest 10 dB, suburban 6 dB, urban 12 dB, and a custom value.

This is one fixed value for the whole path. The planner does not know where the forest really is. If both ends stand in forest, enter the sum (e.g. 2 times 5 dB = 10 dB). If the antenna rises above the treetops, choose open terrain.

Typical values at 868 MHz (orders of magnitude, not measurements): a dozen metres of deciduous forest in summer 5–10 dB, dense conifer forest 10–15 dB or more, less in winter; a housing estate 5–10 dB; dense urban buildings 10–20 dB; plus the walls of a building 10–20 dB if the radio is inside. In the Świętokrzyskie region forests are often 20–30 m tall, so an antenna at 2 m inside them has a clearly limited range even when the terrain itself is no obstacle.

Common mistakes: counting twice (a forest preset and an extra 10 dB by hand) and assuming 0 dB means no obstacles. It is only an assumption. A good method is to tune the value by comparing the prediction with a measurement on a known path (the “Comparison with measurement” card) and to remember it for your area.

Limit: forest and buildings are only approximated by extra attenuation. Gas and rain are added automatically only above 1 GHz.
Terrain profile

The profile is a cross-section of the terrain along the A–B line. The chart shows the terrain with Earth bulge (for the current k), the straight line of sight between the antennas and the first Fresnel zone as a band around it. The horizontal axis is the distance from A, the vertical axis is height ASL.

How it is built: the planner samples the Mapterhorn terrain model at least every 30 m, but at most 400 samples per path, so on paths longer than about 12 km the step grows (about 75 m for 30 km). Heights are interpolated, so narrow obstacles such as a rock or a tower may not show up.

How to read it: if the terrain enters the band or crosses the line of sight, the path is obstructed and the model calculates diffraction (the loss typically rises by a dozen to several tens of dB). Look at the worst point: the planner gives the clearance there in metres and as a fraction of the Fresnel radius. The worst point decides, not the average.

How to use it in practice: raise the antenna on the side closer to the obstacle, because that is where you gain the most clearance. A hill right in front of an antenna is a different problem from the same hill in the middle of the path. You can save the chart as PNG and the data as CSV.

Limits: the profile is one-dimensional. It does not see forest, buildings or obstacles beside the line, and it does not model reflections (e.g. from a slope). Reliability depends on the accuracy of the terrain model.
Fresnel zone

The first Fresnel zone is an ellipsoidal region around the line of sight through which most of the wave energy passes. Its radius is r = √(λ·d1·d2/(d1+d2)), where d1 and d2 are the distances from the ends of the path. For 868 MHz (λ ≈ 0.345 m) at mid-path: 5 km gives about 21 m, 10 km about 29 m, 20 km about 42 m.

Rule of thumb: for the path to behave almost like free space, keep at least 60 percent of the radius clear (on a 10 km path that is about 17–18 m). An obstacle reaching exactly the line of sight already causes about 6 dB of diffraction loss, and one blocking the line much more.

The planner shows the ratio of clearance to radius at the worst point: 1 or more means the zone is clear, 0.6 is a reasonable minimum, 0 means an obstacle touching the line, and a negative value means the path is obstructed. This is an aid for judgement. ITM computes the diffraction effects itself and does not use this indicator as an input.

How to improve it: raise one or both antennas, move the point or change direction. Remember that forest also intrudes into the zone even though you cannot see it on the profile. You represent its effect with the extra attenuation.

Common mistake: judging only by being able to “see the other side”. Optical visibility does not mean a clear Fresnel zone, and at 868 MHz especially the zone is wide, tens of metres in radius.
Link result

The result shows, for both directions (A→B and B→A), the received power, the margin and the verdict. The budget is: received power = transmit power + transmit antenna gain − transmit feeder loss − path loss + receive antenna gain − receive feeder loss. The path loss is the ITM loss plus the extra attenuation (forest and buildings; gas and rain only above 1 GHz). For comparison the planner also gives the free-space loss, the ITM propagation mode (line of sight, diffraction or tropospheric scatter), the distance, bearings and antenna angles.

Example (10 km, clear line of sight, 868 MHz, 20 dBm, 2.15 dBi antennas, no cables): loss about 111 dB, received power about −87 dBm, and with a sensitivity of −127.5 dBm the margin is about 40 dB. Add forest (10 dB) and diffraction over a hill (often several tens of dB) and the margin drops to a few dB or below zero.

A→B and B→A differ only when the powers, antennas or cables at the two ends differ. The path loss is reciprocal.

Warnings: when ITM reports values outside its recommended range (e.g. very low antennas), the result is less reliable. A calculation error gives the verdict “no link”.

Honesty: ITM returns a median value (50 percent of time, locations and situations). The real level in any given minute fluctuates around the prediction, typically by ±6–10 dB. This is a prediction, not a guarantee of coverage.
Link margin and verdict

The margin is the difference between the received power and the receiver sensitivity, in dB. A positive margin means the signal should be decoded; the larger it is, the more robust the link is against fluctuations.

Verdict thresholds: at least 20 dB is excellent, at least 10 dB is good, at least 3 dB is marginal, at least 0 dB is weak, and below 0 dB is no link.

Why so much: the ITM prediction is a median, while the real signal changes with the weather, the season (leaves!), traffic (cars, people), moisture on the antenna and interference. A link with a 3 dB margin will work only sometimes, with 10 dB most of the time, and with 20 dB reliably even in changing conditions. In deciduous forest, on paths through valleys and in spring, plan for 15–20 dB.

How to improve the result, cheapest first: antenna height on the obstacle side (several to a dozen dB), a shorter or better cable (1–3 dB), a higher-gain antenna (3–6 dB), and power last (+3 dB is twice the power, within the regulations).

Common mistakes: looking at one direction only (in a mesh both count, judge the worse one) and treating a positive margin as a guarantee of delivery. Packet collisions and channel load are not modelled.
Bearing and antenna angle

The bearing is the direction from one point to the other, in degrees from north (0° is north, 90° is east). The planner gives the A→B and B→A bearings along the great circle, relative to true (geographic) north. A phone compass and a hand compass usually show magnetic north. The difference is the magnetic declination: in Poland in 2026 it is roughly +5° to +6° (east). This is an approximate value, check it locally (e.g. with the NOAA declination calculator or a compass app). With east declination, magnetic bearing = true bearing − declination, e.g. 90° true is about 84° magnetic.

The antenna (elevation) angle is the vertical tilt towards the other station, computed from the ASL heights of both antennas and the distance, with a correction for Earth curvature (dependent on k). For a 10 km path and the other antenna 100 m higher it comes to about +0.5°. The angle ignores terrain: when a hill obstructs the path it points at the other antenna, not in the direction the energy actually arrives from (after diffraction at an edge).

In practice: omni antennas are mounted vertically, the angle does not matter. Aim Yagis and panels using the bearing to within about ±10°. The beam is usually 20–60° wide, so angles below 1° are generally ignored.

Common mistakes: confusing true and magnetic north (5–6° of error, which already matters with a narrow 20° Yagi beam) and reading the bearing the wrong way round (A→B instead of B→A).
Comparison with measurement

When one end of the link is a mesh node (not yours) and the other is your connected station, the planner compares the prediction with the last measurement: the RSSI (received power in dBm) and the SNR (signal-to-noise ratio in dB) of the last packet from that node. The predicted RSSI is the computed received power in the direction from the node to your station, and the predicted SNR is that RSSI minus the noise level (−174 + 10·log10(BW) + NF). The difference is measurement minus prediction: a negative value means conditions in the field are worse than predicted.

The RSSI is corrected by the LNA gain set in the app, so that the power at the antenna is compared rather than the reading at the chip input. If the correction is not set or is wrong, the difference shifts by the same amount.

How to read it: a difference within ±6 dB is inside the typical ITM spread. A measurement 10–20 dB worse usually means an obstacle that was not accounted for (forest, a building), a worse cable or antenna than assumed, or an overstated gain. A measurement better than predicted suggests reflections or favourable refraction. Use the difference to calibrate the extra attenuation for your area.

Limits: a measurement is a single packet, so average several. Only packets that arrived are visible, so at the edge of range the result is skewed towards better values. A node more than 0 hops away does not describe a direct radio link, and the planner marks this as no direct measurement. The real noise is often higher than the computed one, so the measured SNR can be lower than predicted even when the RSSI agrees.
Coverage around a station

Coverage mode calculates a coverage map around a selected point (A or B). The planner casts radials around the station (72 by default, every 5°) and on each one calculates the ITM loss at about 40 distances up to the chosen maximum (30 km by default). The receiver defaults to 2 m height and 0 dBi gain, which you can change. The colour of a cell shows the margin against sensitivity, from good to no coverage.

How to use it: pick the station, set a maximum range close to realistic expectations (10–20 km for a rooftop radio in the Świętokrzyskie region; a longer range lengthens the calculation), run it and compare with the node map. The result helps choose a place for a new node: look for a location that sees a lot of area towards your users, not just one valley.

Accuracy: between radials values are interpolated, and the spacing grows with distance (at 5° it is about 2.6 km at 30 km), so narrow terrain shadows may vanish. Terrain is sampled about every 200 m. Forest and buildings enter as the same fixed extra attenuation as in the link, and k and N0 come from the last link calculation.

Limits: the map assumes the selected station transmits and the receiver is typical. The reverse direction depends on the power and antenna of the other side. Coverage also depends on the preset: Narrow has about 4 dB less margin than Long Fast. This is a statistical prediction, not a guarantee.
Exporting results

You can save the results in several formats.

PDF: a report with the point data, radio parameters, link result, profile chart, optionally the coverage map, notes, source information and a disclaimer. Good for documentation or for sending to someone.

CSV: numeric data, i.e. the terrain profile (distance, ground, line of sight, Fresnel zone bounds) and a summary. The separator is a semicolon, the decimal separator is a point, and line endings are CRLF. When opening in Excel or LibreOffice, choose the semicolon as the field separator.

KML: points, the link line and, if calculated, coverage samples for Google Earth and other maps.

GeoJSON: points, the line and coverage samples (with margin_db and color fields) for QGIS and web tools. Coordinates are in longitude, latitude order (WGS-84).

PNG: an image of the terrain profile chart.

Before sharing files remember they contain the exact coordinates of your points (e.g. your home or mast). Do not publish them if you do not want to reveal the location. The results are a prediction, and the report carries a disclaimer that it is not a guarantee of coverage. Common problems: a CSV opened with the wrong separator looks like a single column, and a KML with thousands of coverage samples can be heavy for older apps.
